prompt: In the Reno curve, cwnd rises beyond the capacity line while no loss is reported. Assuming the bottleneck capacity stays fixed, what is the main effect of those additional outstanding packets?

options.text: They increase propagation speed along the path.
They increase queue occupancy and queueing delay.
They permanently increase the bottleneck link rate.
They increase the receiver’s advertised buffer size.

explanation: Once the path is filled, extra in-flight packets mostly build a bottleneck queue rather than raise its service rate. Loss-based Reno can continue increasing until a congestion signal causes a reduction.

illustrations.alt: A congestion-window curve rises above a capacity line toward a queue limit, then drops after losses.
illustrations.caption: TCP Reno · PDF page 12

prompt: In this TCP timeline, repeated ACK 1 arrive after later segments get through. What extra information would SACK provide to help recover multiple losses?

options.text: The receive timestamps of every retransmitted segment.
The maximum route capacity inferred by each router.
The received byte ranges beyond the cumulative ACK gap.
The application message boundaries in the received data.

explanation: The cumulative ACK identifies the next missing byte but does not describe all later received ranges. SACK reports those ranges, helping the sender identify and retransmit missing data selectively.

illustrations.alt: A sender–receiver timeline with numbered TCP segments, missing transmissions, and repeated ACK 1.
illustrations.caption: TCP recovery · PDF page 19

prompt: A and C cannot sense each other, but both can reach B. Both perform carrier sensing before transmitting to B. What can happen?

options.text: Both transmit after sensing an idle channel, and their signals collide at B.
Both detect the other’s transmission, so B receives strictly alternating frames.
Only B’s carrier sensing matters, so neither sender needs a backoff procedure.
Both transmissions succeed because separate senders imply separate channels.

explanation: Carrier sensing is local to each sender. A and C may each observe an idle medium while their transmissions interfere at the shared receiver B: the hidden-terminal problem.

illustrations.alt: Wireless stations A and C on opposite sides of an obstacle transmit toward B.
illustrations.caption: Wireless week 2 · PDF page 6

prompt: Compare the two antenna patterns. Which change produces a stronger lobe toward one receiver without increasing the total transmitted data rate by itself?

options.text: Assigning a different destination IP address to every antenna.
Giving every stream an independent transport receive window.
Replacing each antenna weight with a randomly chosen packet route.
Coordinating relative antenna phases and amplitudes for that direction.

explanation: Beamforming combines antenna contributions constructively in a desired direction. It changes the spatial energy pattern; sending independent spatial streams is a separate multiplexing decision.

illustrations.alt: Two antenna radiation patterns: one spreads energy broadly and the other has a directed main lobe.
illustrations.caption: Wireless week 2 · PDF page 16

prompt: The access point serves several stations using spatial beams on one channel. Which condition is important for separating their streams?

options.text: Every station must receive an identical copy of the same payload.
The channels must provide usable spatial separation and suitable channel information.
Every station must share one MAC address throughout the transmission.
The access point must disable coordination between its antennas.

explanation: MU-MIMO uses spatial resources to separate users. It requires suitable channel conditions and sufficiently accurate channel information; multiple antennas alone do not guarantee independent usable streams.

illustrations.alt: A multi-antenna access point sends separate spatial beams to several stations.
illustrations.caption: Wireless week 2 · PDF page 19

prompt: Suppose two subflows between A and H cross the same bottleneck as one ordinary TCP connection. Why couple their congestion controllers?

options.text: To force both subflows to use identical rates even on disjoint bottlenecks.
To let either subflow ignore loss whenever the other one receives an ACK.
To avoid giving the MPTCP connection the aggregate aggressiveness of two competitors.
To reserve the bottleneck exclusively for whichever endpoint has more addresses.

explanation: Independent TCP-like subflows could obtain roughly two flows’ share against one competitor. Coupled control aims to avoid that unfair aggregate advantage while exploiting different paths when appropriate.

illustrations.alt: A network graph connects multihomed endpoint A to endpoint H through intermediate nodes.
illustrations.caption: Network architecture · PDF page 38

prompt: The first HTTP/1.1 pipelined response takes much longer to generate than the next two. The later responses are ready. What prevents sending their complete responses first on this connection?

options.text: HTTP/1.1 requires pipelined responses to follow request order.
HTTP/1.1 permits only one outstanding request per connection.
TCP requires each request to open a separate connection.
TCP requires all three responses to have the same length.

explanation: Pipelining permits multiple outstanding requests, but HTTP/1.1 response ordering still causes application-layer head-of-line blocking. A later ready response waits behind an earlier one.

illustrations.alt: Client–server timeline for pipelined HTTP/1.1 requests and ordered responses.
illustrations.caption: HTTP/1.1 pipelining · PDF page 41
illustrations.credit: High Performance Browser Networking · Ilya Grigorik

prompt: Frames from streams 1, 3 and 5 share the HTTP/2 connection. A TCP segment containing stream 1 data is lost, while later stream 3 bytes arrive. What can still block stream 3 delivery?

options.text: The HTTP/2 frame format has no field identifying a stream.
The server must finish every stream 1 response before sending stream 3 frames.
Each HTTP/2 stream waits for a new independent TCP handshake.
The gap in TCP’s shared ordered byte stream can hold back later bytes.

explanation: HTTP/2 can interleave frames from different streams, removing HTTP/1.1 response serialization. Its TCP connection still delivers one ordered byte stream, so a gap can stall later bytes belonging to other streams.

illustrations.alt: HTTP/2 frames from streams 1, 3 and 5 share one connection between a client and server.
illustrations.caption: HTTP/2 multiplexing · PDF page 54
illustrations.credit: High Performance Browser Networking · Ilya Grigorik

prompt: In the QUIC case, stream A loses data but all data needed to deliver stream B have arrived. Which statement best describes the remaining dependency?

options.text: B must wait for A because QUIC exposes only one ordered byte stream.
B can be delivered, although future transmissions can still share congestion limits.
B can be delivered because QUIC never retransmits missing stream data.
B needs another UDP socket before its received data can be delivered.

explanation: QUIC provides ordered delivery within each reliable stream rather than across all streams together. Complete stream B data need not wait for A; shared congestion control and capacity can still affect subsequent transmissions.

illustrations.alt: HTTP/2 over TCP and QUIC diagrams show several streams and a lost packet.
illustrations.caption: QUIC stream delivery · PDF page 74
illustrations.credit: Diagram credited to devopedia.org/quic in the lecture

prompt: Assume equal-capacity links. Why can the mesh in the middle carry more traffic across the shown balanced cut than the tree on the left?

options.text: Its endpoints have different names on opposite sides of the cut.
Its routes contain no intermediate switches or routers.
Several links cross its cut rather than a single tree link.
Its packets no longer compete for any network resources.

explanation: Bisection capacity sums link capacity across a balanced cut. The pictured tree has a one-link bottleneck; the mesh cut crosses several links. This comparison does not guarantee every traffic pattern achieves that capacity.

illustrations.alt: A tree, a 4-by-4 mesh, and a hypercube are shown with lines dividing their nodes into halves.
illustrations.caption: Interconnection topologies · PDF page 34

prompt: Suppose each packet holds its current channel buffer while requesting the next channel in the dependency cycle. None can release its held buffer first. What makes this a deadlock risk?

options.text: A cycle of hold-and-wait dependencies can prevent every packet in the cycle from advancing.
A cycle proves that packets are moving indefinitely without ever approaching a destination.
A cycle makes routing impossible even when every channel buffer is completely empty.
A cycle means that every packet must have been delivered to the wrong endpoint.

explanation: Deadlock requires more than a geometric cycle: occupied resources and blocking dependencies matter. Under these assumptions, each packet waits for a resource held by another packet in the cycle. Restricting channel dependencies or using suitable virtual channels can prevent such waiting cycles.

illustrations.alt: Packets occupy channels in a mesh; a corresponding directed channel-dependency graph contains cycles.
illustrations.caption: Routing dependencies · PDF page 57

prompt: A core router forwards the packet represented by this MPLS stack. Which label does it normally examine first?

options.text: The innermost service label nearest the payload.
Every label simultaneously to form a transport port.
The original Layer 3 destination instead of any label.
The outermost label at the top of the stack.

explanation: Core MPLS forwarding normally uses the top label. Inner labels can identify additional services or forwarding contexts; the bottom-of-stack bit identifies the last label before the payload.

illustrations.alt: An MPLS stack showing LDP, TE and VPN labels above a Layer 2/3 packet header.
illustrations.caption: MPLS label stack · PDF page 26

prompt: Both senders may have enough window space for all the shown packets. What does pacing change relative to sending them as a burst?

options.text: It increases the maximum size of every packet on the link.
It spaces transmissions to reduce short-term queue spikes.
It eliminates the need to obey the congestion window.
It guarantees an identical end-to-end delay for every packet.

explanation: A window limits how much data may be outstanding; pacing also regulates when packets enter the path. Spreading transmissions can reduce microbursts without guaranteeing latency or replacing congestion control.

illustrations.alt: Two sender–receiver diagrams compare closely bunched packets with evenly spaced packets.
illustrations.caption: Pacing · PDF page 37

prompt: The vertical feature is rescaled while the horizontal feature is left unchanged. What can change when kNN uses Euclidean distance after this transformation?

options.text: Only the printed tick labels change; nearest-neighbor order must remain identical.
Every class label is rescaled by the same factor as the vertical feature.
The relative contribution of the vertical feature and the resulting neighbor ranking can change.
Every distance becomes equal because normalization removes all variation.

explanation: Rescaling one coordinate changes its contribution to Euclidean distance. Points retain their labels, but nearest-neighbor rankings and predictions can change. Fit scaling parameters on training data and reuse them on validation or test data.

illustrations.alt: Two scatter plots show the same points before and after the vertical axis is rescaled.
illustrations.caption: Feature scaling · week 3, PDF page 18

prompt: The join-the-dots model fits the displayed training points exactly. What is the soundest way to decide whether it generalizes better than the quadratic model?

options.text: Compare performance on validation data using the same evaluation procedure.
Select join-the-dots solely because its training error is smallest.
Select the model with the greatest number of adjustable parameters.
Tune both models repeatedly against the final test labels until one wins.

explanation: Training fit alone cannot establish generalization. Use held-out validation or cross-validation for model selection, then reserve the test set for evaluating the selected procedure.

illustrations.alt: The same data are fitted by a straight line, a quadratic curve, and a join-the-dots curve.
illustrations.caption: Model selection · week 10, PDF page 16
